transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um... I guess I’m here because I just can’t seem to get past this one thing, and it’s really starting to wear me down. It’s my face. Well, more specifically, my jaw and my neck area. There is this... this sagging, incredibly uneven spot right along the jawline that just looks awful. I mean, I'll be getting ready for work—I do personal care, mostly helping out elderly folks, so I’m always interacting with people—and I just can't stop seeing it. 

And once I'm out of the house, I just know it’s the very first thing anyone sees. When I’m talking to the families of my clients, or consulting with the visiting nurses, I can almost feel their eyes darting right to that exact spot on my neck. It’s humiliating, honestly. And it’s not just at work, it happens on Sundays too. I’ll be at church, trying to focus on the service or talking to people at coffee hour, but I’m just convinced everyone is noticing how lopsided and saggy my skin is right there. I’ve brought it up to folks, but everyone just brushes it off. They tell me it looks completely normal, that they don't see what I'm talking about, but I know they’re just trying to spare my feelings. Because how could they not see it? It's right there, and it's all I can focus on no matter where I am or what I'm doing.
Is it only your jaw and neck area that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that you also worry about?

You know, I’ve thought about that, and... no, it’s really just the jaw and the neck. I mean, I’m 48 years old, so I know my body is going to change, right? I’m on my feet all day, lifting my clients, helping them transition from the bed to the wheelchair or the bath, so I’ve always been pretty sturdy and I'm honestly completely okay with that. My arms are fine, my legs do what they need to do, and I don't really pay much attention to my weight or my stomach or anything like that. I've always just been kind of average-looking overall, which is perfectly fine by me! I really don't need to look like a movie star or anything. 

But it’s just... it's this one specific area. It’s like all my focus just zeroes right in on that lower half of my face. Sometimes I’ll be getting ready in the morning and I’ll look in the mirror and try to just look at my eyes, or maybe my hair—I actually have pretty nice hair, it's always been thick, which is a blessing from my mother's side of the family—but my eyes just drag right down to that sagging, uneven skin on my jawline. It’s like a magnet, I just can't look away from it. 

So, no, I don't really sit around worrying about my nose or my thighs or my hands or anything else. If I could just wake up tomorrow and have this one awful, lopsided part of my neck look normal like everyone else's, I swear to you I wouldn't complain about a single other thing on my body. It’s just this one spot, but it's so bad that it feels like it ruins everything else.
Has your concern about your jaw and neck area affected your ability to interact with people or perform your job as a personal care worker?

Well, yes, it... it really has. I mean, I love my job, I truly do. I've been doing personal care for over fifteen years now, and I care so deeply about my clients. But lately, this whole thing with my jaw, it’s just getting in the way of everything. For instance, my agency has these monthly staff meetings, and recently my supervisor actually asked if I’d be willing to help lead some of the training sessions for the new hires, or maybe take on some of the supervisory pieces, you know, checking in on the other aides. And I had to say no. I just passed it up. Because the thought of standing up there at the front of the room, or sitting across from a new girl trying to explain protocols... all I could think about was how they’d just be staring right at my neck the whole time. I just couldn't stomach it. 

And it's affecting my day-to-day work, too, honestly. The paperwork—oh, the paperwork in this job is endless, you have to document every little thing, every medication, every meal. And I’ve actually fallen behind on it. Not because I don't know how to do it, but because in the mornings, I get so stuck in front of the mirror. I’ll spend I don't even know how long, just trying different collars, different scarves, trying to contour with makeup—which I’m not even good at!—just trying to make myself look halfway presentable so the sagging isn't the only thing people see. By the time I finally leave the house, I'm rushing, and then the paperwork just piles up. 

It’s not just work, either. It’s bleeding into my personal life. I used to be so active. I’ve been part of this wonderful book club for years, we meet every other Tuesday, and I was in a walking club on Saturday mornings with some ladies from my neighborhood. But... I’ve stopped going to a lot of those things. The getting ready part, the anticipating how everyone is going to look at me, it just feels like entirely too much effort. It’s exhausting. It’s just easier to stay home where I don't have to worry about the lighting or the angle of my face when I talk. It's just... it's taking over, you know?
Do you think it's possible that your jaw and neck area actually look normal to other people, and it's just your own perception that it looks uneven?

I hear what you are asking, I really do. And I know I brought this up a few minutes ago, about how folks tell me it looks normal. My sister, for instance, she came over just this past Sunday. I had made a pot roast, it is a recipe from our grandmother and it takes all afternoon, so we were sitting at the kitchen island waiting on it, and I asked her if the overhead lighting was making the lopsided part of my neck cast a weird shadow. And she swore up and down that she didn't see a single thing wrong. She told me I look completely fine and that I need to stop worrying about it. 

But... I just cannot wrap my head around that. I mean, the whole reason I came in to see you today is because I just cannot stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot around my jaw and my neck. It is right there. It is so glaring. So when you ask if it is just my perception, I try to tell myself maybe you are right, maybe my sister is right, but then I catch my reflection in the bathroom mirror, or even just in the window of my car when I am backing out of the driveway, and it is all I can see. 

And because I see it so clearly, I just feel it deep down that it is the absolute first thing the families of my clients notice when they look at me. Or the visiting nurses. Or the people at church. They might be smiling and telling me to have a blessed day, or going over a medication chart with me, but I just know their eyes are drawn to it. Even if they are too polite to say it to my face, I feel like they have to be seeing it, because how could they not? It is just so obvious to me, so I just... I can't believe it when people say it looks normal. I really can't. It just feels like they are trying to be nice, you know? Because to me, it is huge.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your jaw and neck area is not based on how it actually looks?

I... I mean, I guess anything in this world is possible, right? But... I just don't see how that could be the case. I really don't. Because, well, let me give you an example. Just the other day, I was at work with one of my clients—Mrs. Higgins, she’s 82, such a sweet lady, I’ve been helping her out for about three years now—and her daughter came to visit and wanted to take a picture of the two of us out on the sun porch. And of course, I smiled for the camera, but the whole time my stomach was just in absolute knots. And when she showed me the picture on her phone? I zoomed right in on my jaw. I didn't even look at Mrs. Higgins's sweet face, God forgive me, I just looked straight at my own neck. And it was right there. The sagging, the way it droops so much more on that one side... it wasn't just in my head. It was right there on the little screen. 

So when you ask if my perception isn't based on how it actually looks... I just get so confused by that. Because my eyes are seeing it. I'll stand in my bathroom—and I know the fluorescent lights in there are just awful, they show every little flaw on a person, my sister always complains about them too—but I'll stand there and I'll actually take my fingers and just gently pull the skin back on my jawline, just a fraction of an inch, just to see what it would look like if it were normal and tight like it's supposed to be. And the difference is just night and day. It’s like a completely different face looking back at me. 

If my brain is somehow tricking me into seeing something that isn't there, it is doing a really, really good job of it. Because to me, it is as real as this chair I'm sitting in right now. I try to tell myself, you know, 'Okay, maybe it's just a bad angle today,' or 'Maybe you're just exhausted from working a twelve-hour shift and lifting wheelchairs all day,' but then I look in the mirror again, and it's still just as bad. It never changes. So... I don't know. I just really, really struggle to believe that it's just my perception when I can see it so plainly with my own two eyes.
Do you think there's any possibility, no matter how small, that your jaw and neck area actually look normal, but you're just seeing it differently?

I know you're trying to help me see it another way, Doctor, and I appreciate that, I really do. But... I mean, like I was saying just a few minutes ago, the entire reason I even made this appointment and came in to see you today is exactly because I just cannot stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot around my jaw and my neck. It is just constantly, constantly on my mind. It never goes away. 

So when you ask if there is even a tiny possibility that it looks normal... I want to say yes, just to give you the answer you're looking for, but honestly? No. I just can't see that possibility. Because even when folks tell me it looks normal, like my sister did on Sunday, my brain just absolutely will not accept it. I just feel—well, no, I don't just feel it, I *know* it—that it is the very first thing people notice when they look at me. 

Like I mentioned before, when I'm dealing with the families of my clients, or when the visiting nurses come to the house to check vitals and we have to stand there face-to-face to go over the charts... I can just feel their eyes darting right to that droop. Or even just the people at my church! Oh, at church, it's just terrible lately. I've actually started sitting near the back, usually on the left side, because the stained glass window on the right lets in this harsh morning light that I just know highlights the sagging on my jaw. I'll sit there on Sunday mornings, and I try so, so hard to just listen to Pastor Davis and be present in the service, but all I can think about is how the usher handing me the bulletin is staring right at my neck. Or how the people in the pews around me can see the unevenness when I turn my head to sing the hymns. It's just... it is the first thing they see. It has to be, because it's so huge to me. 

So, a possibility that I'm just seeing it differently and everyone else sees a normal neck? I just... I can't get there. I just really, truly don't think I can believe that.
Have you ever considered that your perception of your jaw and neck area might be entirely inaccurate, and that there might not be any actual sagging or unevenness?

Doctor, I feel like we might be going around in circles just a little bit here, and I truly don't mean any disrespect by saying that, I really don't, but... I just don't know how else to explain it. Like I keep saying, I just can't consider that. I really can't. I know I’ve said this already, but the entire reason I even came in to see you today, the whole reason I made this appointment and actually took a morning off work—which is not an easy thing to do when you have elderly clients depending on you to help them out of bed and get their breakfast going—is exactly because I just cannot stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot around my jaw and my neck. It is just constantly there, staring right back at me. 

So to try and tell myself that it might be entirely inaccurate, that there isn't any actual sagging at all... I just don't know how a person does that. Because even when folks tell me it looks normal, it just doesn't change a single thing for me. It doesn't change what I see, and it definitely doesn't change how I feel when I have to interact with people. Like I was telling you before about the families of my clients, or the visiting nurses who come by the house, or all the people at my church... I still just feel it, deep down in my bones, that this droop is the absolute first thing they notice when they look at me. 

I know you're asking if it's possible that it's just not there, but when I feel so strongly that everyone else is staring right at it, whether they're handing me a hymnal or going over a blood pressure reading with me... how could I ever believe it's not real? I'm the one living with it, looking at it every single day, so I just... I can't consider that it's all in my head. I just can't.
Has your concern about your jaw and neck area caused you to avoid any specific social situations or activities that you would normally enjoy?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It really has... it's just taken over so much of my life, Doctor. I mean, work is a big one. I love my job, I really do, and I've been doing personal care for a long time, so I know what I'm doing. My supervisor actually brought up the idea a few months ago about me taking on some supervisory pieces, maybe helping to lead some of the staff meetings or training the new aides when they come on board. And you know, a few years ago, I would have jumped at that. I would have been so proud. But I passed it up. I just made up some excuse about my schedule being too full, but the real reason—the only reason—is because the thought of standing up at the front of a room, under those bright fluorescent office lights, with all those people just staring right at my face and my neck... I couldn't do it. My stomach just drops even thinking about it. And it's affecting my regular work, too. I've actually fallen behind on my paperwork a few times lately, not because I don't know how to do it, but because I get so stuck in the morning trying to get ready. I'll spend so much time in front of the mirror, trying to arrange my hair or find a scarf that hides the droop just right, trying to make myself look presentable enough to even walk out the door, that I end up running late and the paperwork just piles up. 

And it's not just work, either. It's my personal life, too. I used to be so active with my friends. We have this little book club that meets once a month on Tuesday evenings, usually at someone's house, and we always put out a nice spread of cheese and crackers and just talk for hours. And I'm also part of a walking club that meets at the park on Saturday mornings. We'd walk the trail and then get coffee after. But lately... I've just stopped going to a lot of those things. Getting ready for them just feels like this massive, exhausting chore. The whole time I'm trying to get dressed, I'm just staring at my jaw, trying to figure out if it looks worse today than it did yesterday, and by the time I'm supposed to leave, I'm just so drained and anxious that it feels like too much. I'll just text them and say I have a migraine or I'm too tired from work. I miss them, I really do, and I miss reading the books and talking about them, but the idea of sitting in a living room with everyone looking at me, or being out in the bright morning sun at the park... I just can't do it. It's just easier to stay home where no one can see me.
Have you ever considered seeking a professional opinion, such as a dermatologist or plastic surgeon, to evaluate the appearance of your jaw and neck area?

A dermatologist? Or... a plastic surgeon? Oh, wow. Um, no, I... I haven't really thought about doing something like that. I mean, I haven't looked into it at all. 

I guess... well, I'm just a personal care aide, you know? I make a decent living, but I certainly don't have the kind of money just lying around for big cosmetic procedures. It always just felt like something that people on television do, or ladies with a lot of money, not someone like me who's just trying to make sure Mrs. Higgins gets her morning medications on time. 

And honestly, Doctor, I think I'd just be entirely too mortified to even sit in a plastic surgeon's waiting room. Can you imagine? Me, sitting there under those bright lights they always have in those fancy offices, having to point out this awful, uneven droop to a doctor whose whole entire job is to look at faces all day? I think I would just die of embarrassment before I even made it back to the examination room. I get anxious enough just having the visiting nurses look at me at work, let alone a doctor who specializes in how things are supposed to look. 

So I've just been trying to handle it myself, really. I don't even want to admit to you how much money I've spent at the pharmacy down the street from my house. I'll go in there after my shift, when my feet are just aching from standing all day, and I'll stand in the skincare aisle for what feels like hours. I read the back of every single jar and bottle—the firming creams, the lifting serums, the ones with collagen and whatever else they put in there that promises to tighten up sagging skin. I buy them, and I bring them home, and I stand in front of the bathroom mirror applying them exactly like the directions say, doing these upward strokes because they say you have to fight gravity. I spend so much time rubbing those creams into my jaw and my neck, just praying it'll make a difference. 

But it never works. It never changes anything. The sagging is still right there. But even so, going to a surgeon or a skin doctor... no, I haven't considered that. I just keep buying the creams and trying to find the right scarves to cover it up, even though it's exhausting. It really is just so exhausting.
Do you think someone who did not know you and saw you for the first time would notice this sagging on your jaw and neck?

Oh, absolutely. Without a shadow of a doubt. I know I was rambling a bit about this earlier when I mentioned the visiting nurses and the folks at my church, but it goes for strangers, too. Honestly, I think strangers might even notice it more, or at least I feel so much more exposed around them. 

Like, if I just need to run into the grocery store after a long shift—just a quick trip to grab some milk or maybe some bread for the week—I absolutely dread getting to the checkout line. I'll walk up to the cashier, someone who has never laid eyes on me before in their entire life, and I just... I know they see it. I can feel their eyes darting right down to my jawline while they're scanning my items. 

Because, like I keep saying—and I know I probably sound like a broken record today, but it really is the whole reason I came in to see you—I just cannot stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot. It is so glaringly obvious to me, it's just hanging right there. So even when well-meaning folks in my life try to pat my hand and tell me it looks normal, it doesn't mean a single thing when I'm standing in front of a complete stranger. I'll be standing there under those awful store lights, fumbling with my purse, trying to get my debit card out, and my face just burns because I know, I just know deep down, that this droop is the absolute first thing they notice. 

They aren't looking at my eyes, they aren't looking at my smile, they're looking right at my neck. It’s like a neon sign pointing right at it. So yes, whether it's a new family member of a client I'm meeting for the very first time, or a cashier, or just a random person passing me on the sidewalk... I feel it in my bones that they see exactly what I see the second they look at me.
Have you ever had a moment where you doubted your perception of the sagging on your jaw and neck?

Doubted it? Like... thought maybe it wasn't really there, or wasn't as bad as I think? Oh, no. No, Doctor, never. I mean, I truly, truly wish I could say yes to that. I wish I could wake up just one morning and look in the mirror and think, 'Oh, maybe I'm just making a mountain out of a molehill,' but... I just can't. Because it's right there. It is just a plain fact. 

I know I mentioned my friends and folks at church trying to tell me I look fine, and bless their hearts, I know they're just trying to be kind to me. But they don't see what I see when I'm alone in my bathroom. I actually... well, a couple of weeks ago, I went down to the hardware store and bought three different kinds of lightbulbs. I thought, well, maybe it's just the harsh overhead light in my apartment making the shadows look worse than they really are. So I spent a whole Saturday afternoon changing out the fixtures, trying the soft white bulbs, the warm glow ones, even those bright daylight ones. I was standing on the edge of the bathtub, swapping them out one by one, just praying that with a different light, the sagging wouldn't look so severe. I wanted so badly to prove myself wrong, you know? I wanted to find a reason to doubt it. 

But it didn't matter what bulb I put in. The droop was exactly the same. I'll take my fingers and I'll pull the skin back on my jaw, just gently, up towards my ears, just to see what my face is actually supposed to look like. And for a split second, it looks normal. But the second I let go, it just collapses again. It just hangs there, all uneven and heavy. So how can I doubt it when I can physically see it happening with my own two eyes? 

It's not my imagination. I'll be at work, making a quick lunch for one of my clients—like Mrs. Gable, she loves those little turkey sandwiches with the crusts cut off—and I'll just happen to catch my reflection in the glass of the microwave door or the window over her kitchen sink, and it hits me all over again. It's just so undeniably there, even in a reflection on a microwave. So, no... I don't ever doubt it. I really don't. I just have to live with knowing exactly how awful it looks.
Do you think about your jaw and neck area at all when you are alone and not interacting with anyone?

Oh, Lord, yes. It doesn't just switch off just because there's nobody else in the room with me. I really, really wish it did, but... um, no, it's always there. I'll just be sitting on my couch at night, you know, finally off my feet after a long shift, maybe trying to watch a little television or read a magazine, and my hand just... it just automatically drifts right up to my jawline. I don't even realize I'm doing it half the time. I'll just sit there in my living room, feeling how loose the skin is, pulling at it, completely missing whatever is happening on my show. 

It's honestly... well, I know I'm probably talking your ear off today, and I'm sorry to keep circling back to this, but it really is the whole reason I made this appointment. I came in because I just can’t stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot around my jaw and neck. It just consumes me, whether I'm standing alone in my bathroom or sitting on my couch in the quiet. It’s all I can think about. 

And then, because I spend all night agonizing over it by myself, it makes going out the next day that much harder. Because, like I said before, even when folks try to be sweet and tell me it looks normal, I just... I can't believe them. I feel like it’s the very first thing the families of my clients, the visiting nurses at work, or the people at my church notice when they look at me. So, being alone doesn't give me any peace from it at all. It just gives me more quiet time to obsess over how bad it looks, and to dread having to face all those people the next morning knowing that this awful droop is all they're going to see.
Do you worry that your jaw and neck area affects how people perceive you as a person, beyond just its appearance?

Like my character? Or my personality? Um... well, no, I don't think so. I haven't really thought about it quite like that, to be honest with you. I don't think anyone looks at my jawline and thinks, 'Oh, she must be a terrible person' or 'She's bad at her job.' I really don't. 

Because, you know, I take a whole lot of pride in the work I do. I've been doing personal care for a long time, and I know I have a good heart. I go above and beyond for my folks. I don't just do the bare minimum, you know? Like if I'm over at Mr. Henderson's place—he's another one of my regulars—I don't just make sure he takes his morning pills and leave it at that. I'll sit and listen to his stories about his time in the Navy, or I'll make sure his favorite slippers are right by the bed where he can reach them so his feet don't get cold on the linoleum. And the families of my clients, they see that. They know I'm a good, reliable woman who cares about their loved ones. So I don't think they judge my soul, or my work ethic, or anything deep like that just because of my face. 

It's really just... it's strictly about how awful it looks on the outside. That's what I can't let go of. I just worry that they're staring at the sagging skin and thinking about how old and tired and droopy my face is. Like, they can think I'm the sweetest caregiver in the whole world, and they probably do, but in my head, I'm just agonizing, thinking, 'They're looking right at this horrible hanging skin while I'm talking to them.' 

So, no, it's not about who I am on the inside. I know who I am. It's just... I just can't get past how glaringly obvious this uneven spot is. I know that's exactly what they're seeing the second they look at me, even if they think I'm a perfectly nice lady. It's just the appearance of it that completely consumes me, you know? Not my character.
Do you ever feel compelled to perform specific rituals or routines in an attempt to temporarily alleviate your concerns about the appearance of your jaw and neck area?

Oh, goodness, yes. It's like... well, it's practically a whole production every single morning. I really wish it wasn't, but I just can't seem to help it. 

Before I even step out the door to leave for work, or especially if I have a meeting with my supervisor at the home care agency, I just... I get stuck. I'll get myself all dressed and ready, and I'll think I'm finally done, but then I just keep going back to the bathroom mirror. I can't just look once and walk away. I'll walk down the hall toward the kitchen, stop dead in my tracks, turn right back around, and go look again. 

And while I'm in there, I'm constantly messing with my clothes. I'll spend I don't know how long just fixing my collar, pulling it up just a fraction of an inch, trying to see if it shadows the droop better. Or I'll be fussing with my hair, trying to pull pieces forward around my neck so it covers that uneven spot. I'll brush it one way, then the other, just praying it hides the sagging. 

Then, even when I finally make it to the front door and I've got my purse and my keys, I'll pull out my phone. I'll open up the camera—you know, the front-facing one that you use for pictures of yourself—and I'll take another look, just to see what my neck looks like in the natural light coming through the living room window. 

And my poor daughter, bless her heart, I know I drive her absolutely crazy with it. She'll be trying to eat her breakfast or get ready for her own day, and I'll go over and ask her, "Honey, does this look strange? Can you see it hanging down on this side?" I'll ask her over and over, just hoping she'll say no and that maybe, just maybe, I'll actually believe her for a second. 

And honestly, doctor, it's... well, it's become a real problem because it's made me late. More than once, actually. I'll be so caught up in adjusting my collar, checking my phone camera, and pestering my daughter about how it looks that I end up having to rush like a madwoman to get to my first client's house on time. I hate being late, I really pride myself on being punctual for my folks, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing all this before I leave the house. I just have to try and fix it.
Do you think you would still be concerned about your appearance if the sagging on your jaw and neck area were to somehow be completely fixed?

Oh, wow... um. Goodness, I really don't know. I haven't even let myself think that far ahead, to be completely honest with you. It’s just so hard to even picture a day where I wake up and that awful droop isn't the very first thing staring back at me in the mirror. I mean, if it were just... gone? If it were just completely fixed and smooth, back to how it used to be? I'd like to think I'd be perfectly happy. I'd like to think I could just get up, wash my face, put on my scrubs, and walk right out the door to see my folks without all that fussing and checking my phone camera that I was just telling you about. 

But... would I still be worried about my looks? Would I find something else to fixate on? I just don't know. I really couldn't say. Right now, this jawline thing is just so big, it takes up absolutely all the room in my head. It's like... well, it's like a giant storm cloud, you know? You can't see what's behind the cloud because it's just so dark and heavy and it's parked right over your house. Maybe if the cloud cleared, I'd start worrying about the wrinkles around my eyes, or my hands—you know, working in personal care, my hands get so terribly dry and they're starting to look a little older from all the constant hand-washing and the sanitizing we have to do between clients. 

But I don't agonize over my hands right now. It's just this neck. This uneven, sagging skin. So if you ask me if I'd still be concerned about my appearance if we could just wave a magic wand and fix my jaw... I just don't have a good answer for you, doctor. I really don't. I just pray for the day I could find out, you know? Just to have one single morning where I don't have to pester my poor daughter about how my face looks. Just one morning where I can drink my coffee in peace before my shift without pulling at my collar. I just don't know what I'd feel, or if I'd find something new to hate, but I sure would love the chance to find out.
Do you think you would still find something else about your appearance to worry about if your concern about your jaw and neck area were completely resolved?

Well, like I was trying to say just a minute ago, it's so hard to even imagine that. I guess... I mean, maybe? Human nature being what it is, maybe I'd find a new flaw if this one miraculously disappeared. But honestly, doctor, the whole entire reason I even came in here to talk to you in the first place is just because I absolutely cannot stop seeing this sagging, uneven spot right here around my jaw and my neck. It’s just so prominent to me, it's all I can focus on. 

And the frustrating thing is, even when folks try to reassure me—like my daughter, or my friends, they'll swear up and down that it looks completely normal, that they don't even see what I'm talking about—it just doesn't change anything for me. It doesn't help alleviate the panic. Because in my mind, I just feel like it is the very first thing that the families of my clients notice when I walk through their front door to start my shift. I'll be introducing myself to a new client's daughter, and I can just feel her eyes darting down to my jawline. Or the visiting nurses, when I have to go into the home care office to drop off my paperwork or attend a staff meeting, I just know they're looking at it and analyzing it because they're medical professionals, you know? 

Even the people at my church! I've been going to the same church for years, but lately, I'll be sitting there on a Sunday morning, trying my hardest to just listen to the sermon and find some peace, and if someone turns around in the pew in front of me to say good morning or pass the collection plate, I just freeze. I feel like their eyes go straight to my neck. It's like they're zeroing right in on this droopy skin. 

So when you ask if I'd find something else to worry about... I just can't see past this right now to even give you a proper answer.
